catalog_quote: [Mberia 1993: 180] "As shown in the above data a sequence of underlying /a/ and /e/ gives rise to a phonetic [ɛ] irrespective of whether the two vowels are separated by a morpheme boundary or a word boundary. When the process operates across a word boundary the two words are pronounced as one phonological word marked by a single main stress on the penultinate [sic] syllable." [p. 173] "After the deletion and the gliding processes have taken place, the two adjacent morphological words are pronounced as one phonological word (that is, marked by a single major stress on the penultimate syllable)." [Lindblom 1914: 12] "8. Accent. Grave, as in Swed. vallar (»broken» melody, falling-rising), as well as acute, as in Swed. vallen (falling melody), are found, and the occurrence of the latter, being considerably more abundant than in Kikamba, gives to the language quite a different character. It is particularly marked in the locative, where Kikamba quite as regularly presents grave. ... The principal stress, as in Kikamba, rests as a rule on the penultima. What has further been said concerning the accentuation of the language last referred to, is undoubtedly true also of Kitharaka (vide my »Notes on the Kamba language»)."

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: All three quoted passages are present verbatim at the stated locators, checked on both the extracted text and the rendered page scan Mberia 1993 (254 pp.): p. 184 = printed p. 173 reads "the two adjacent morphological words are pronounced as one phonological word (that is, marked by a single major stress on the penultimate syllable)" (section on vowel deletion before /e/,/o/ + V, ex. 117 /o+ana # o+a+kwa/ -> [mwanwakwa] 'my child'); p. 191 = printed p. 180 reads "When the process operates across a word boundary the two words are pronounced as one phonological word marked by a single main stress on the penultinate [sic, typo for penultimate] syllable" (a+e coalescence, exx. 131-132, incl. a…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Kitharaka is a tone language with lexically distinctive (H/L) tone on verb stems (Mberia 1993, minimal pairs pp. 230-231; also Muriungi 2005, Harford 1997). Independently of tone, a single main (major, principal) stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the phonological word; Mberia uses this penultimate stress as the diagnostic of the phonological word when vowel deletion or a+e coalescence fuses two or three adjacent morphological words. Lindblom 1914 gives the same rule ('as a rule on the penultima') for the word, plus Swedish-style grave/acute word melodies (an early description of tonal contours).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any source; Mberia speaks of 'a single' main/major stress per phonological word.
new_statements.exceptions: None listed. Lindblom hedges with 'as a rule'. Mberia's tone data show that tone, not stress, is contrastive; he states the tonal system was outside his scope and needs research.
new_statements.domain_note: Mberia: the phonological word, which after post-lexical vowel deletion/coalescence may span two or three morphological words (e.g. /o+ana # o+a+kwa/ -> [mwanwakwa] 'my child'); the penult is counted in the fused phonological word. Lindblom: the word in citation/connected speech, no domain discussion. Neither source gives instrumental evidence.
new_statements.identity_note: Both sources describe Kitharaka/Tharaka proper (Glottolog thar1283, ISO thk, Guthrie E54), spoken in Tharaka (Tharaka-Nithi), Kenya; no dialect is singled out. Mberia is a native speaker; Lindblom's 1911-12 data came from two Tharaka men working for him in Machakos, and he treats the language as close to Kikuyu/Meru rather than Kamba. Glottolog alternative names: Kitharaka, Saraka, Sharoka.

tone_statements.citation: Kagaya, Ryohei (1985).. = A tonal analysis of Tharaka nouns in four frames. Journal of Asian and African studies / Ajia Afuriku gengo bunka kenkyu 29. pp. 132-164.
tone_statements.quote: As the result, nouns are divided into five types: (1) L type, (2) HL-I type, (3) LH type, (4) HLH type and (5) HL-II type. ... Basic representations of HL-I, LH and HLH types are distinguished by both the distinctive mark at a syllable boundary which specifies the change from low to high tone, and the inherent function of each type (word tone). ... この言語で音の高低を担って音声上にあらわれてくる単位は，V, CV, (NCV 音節の) N である。... 標準形での表示は高と低のみで充分で，音調形での表示記号を使う。
tone_statements.translation: (Japanese part:) In this language the units that carry pitch and appear phonetically are V, CV, and the N (of an NCV syllable). ... For the standard form, representation with high and low alone is sufficient, and the notation symbols of the tonal form are used.
tone_statements.locator: English summary, pp. 132-133; Japanese sec. 0 はじめに, p. 134, left col. bottom and right col.
tone_statements.summary: Five noun word-tone types (L, HL-I, LH, HLH, HL-II) from H and L on V/CV/N units plus a rise-onset mark at a syllable boundary; extra-high/-low, falling, 'downdrift' phonetic; 40+ forms; no stress.

tone_statements.citation: Ford, K. C. 1976. Tone in Kikamba and the Central Kenya Bantu languages. Studies in African Linguistics 7(3): 261-293.
tone_statements.quote: Certain details of K[ĩ]kamba noun tones are generalisable for the whole group of dialects. i) The distinction of three tonal classes of words (-H#; -HL#; -LL#), based on the quality of final tones, is maintained by all the dialects. Neutralisations of the sub-classification A/B have taken place as follows: (9) a. Tigania: 5 classes ... b. Mĩitine and one dialect of Imenti ...: 4 classes ... c. Tharaka and one dialect of Imenti (Annah Kiambati): 3 classes: -H#; -HL#; -LL# ... [p. 286] The functions of tone in WH-questions in Kĩkamba are the same for all dialects, though again Imenti and Tharaka have neutralised the basic tonal oppositions, both between forms found sentence-finally or not, and between items immediately following a positive declarative verb or not.
